title: Halloween Bars Are Scary Profitable
summary:
Halloween is one of the strongest sales drivers for bars and restaurants. Why not make it last longer?

The post Halloween Bars Are Scary Profitable appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Key Points

  • Pop-up franchises like Black Lagoon help bars extend single-night Halloween crowds into a lucrative, month-long revenue stream.
  • Immersive seasonal menus allow high-end cocktail lounges to attract group traffic and capitalize on holiday spending.
  • Driven by a growing demand for escapism, year-round spooky bars and extended events succeed long after October ends.

For many bargoers, visiting one of the myriad Christmas-themed pop-ups that roll out in December has become an annual rite. Bars count on the business that these programs bring in, too.

Increasingly, hospitality pros are hoping to replicate that magic—and profitability—with Halloween-themed pop-ups that extend beyond spooky season.

For the past six years, a “goth-tropical” franchise called Black Lagoon has been the front-runner in the Halloween bar biz, transforming bars across North America with eerie, cinematic décor and themed drinks like the Moon Shadow (nutmeg-infused vodka, banana liqueur, and cold brew coffee). In 2026, 34 venues are slated to participate.

Co-founded by Erin Hayes and Kelsey Ramage, both based in Los Angeles, Black Lagoon began as a post-pandemic pop-up. 

“We love the witchy vibes, the celebratory aspects of it,” Hayes says. “Kelsey had found a place to rent for the month of October, and it was successful beyond what we had imagined. We had people lined up around the block every night. People loved the weird and wonderful vibe that we were putting out.”

Over time, their pop-up grew into a franchise. Bars pay a fee to rebrand as a Black Lagoon for the month. In turn, they receive creepy tropical mugs and other glassware; a six-drink menu that spotlights a handful of brand sponsors, including Teremana tequila, Kraken rum, and Mr. Black cold brew coffee liqueur; a lookbook for décor; and playlists.

“We try to make it plug-and-play,” Hayes says. “We say, ‘Here are the things you need for your success, now it’s up to you to put it into play.’ They can do whatever they want to dress up the space, we just ask them to keep to the menu.”

Black Lagoon’s success hasn’t gone unnoticed. This year, New York City-based Cocktail Kingdom Hospitality Group, the team behind super popular Christmas-themed pop-ups Miracle and Sippin’ Santa, is getting into the mix with The Haunting, a similar franchise of Halloween-themed immersive pop-up bars.

The mood skews more nostalgic than goth, leaning into childhood haunted houses for aesthetic inspiration and trick-or-treat bags for drinks like the Scream-sicle (tequila, spiced vanilla liqueur, carrot and orange cordial, and habanero). 

About 40 bars—most of which are already part of the Miracle franchise—are slated to participate in the month-long pop-up. There are locations across the United States and in London and Oslo. The business model is similar to Miracle and Black Lagoon: bars pay a fee to participate, and receive recipes and physical menus (unlike Black Lagoon, brand sponsors are not designated), social media assets, and branded merch. The latter includes mugs resembling colorful cauldrons or creepy doll heads, created by Cocktail Kingdom and available for purchase.

Treats for Some Bars, Tricks for Others

Halloween presents an oddly uneven playing ground for bars.

For traditional bars and taverns, it’s a bonanza: The Saturday before or after Halloween consistently ranks among the top ten days of the year for drinking venues in the U.S., according to Nielsen’s NIQ BeverageTrak. 

In 2025, it was the eighth busiest night of the year, as measured by sales value at the average outlet. It ranked behind St. Patrick’s Day in the number-one spot, as well as sports events like the official kickoff of the MLB Division Series, March Madness, and the NFL regular season opening week.

“Halloween is one of the strongest sales drivers for bars and restaurants because it turns a night out into a full-fledged occasion,” says Matt Crompton, vice president of On Premise for NIQ. 

The occasion gives people a specific reason to go out, particularly in groups, so bars see higher-than-normal amounts of weekend traffic. Consumers are willing to spend more on themed cocktails and other premium drinks, too. 

“Combined with broad appeal across age groups and the amplifying power of social media, Halloween consistently ranks among the top revenue-generating days of the year for drinking venues,” Crompton says.

However, intimate bars that focus on high-end drinks typically don’t see the same results, says Greg Boehm, founder and CEO of Cocktail Kingdom Hospitality Group. “Halloween is a bad night for cocktail bars.” 

The Miracle team is hoping a monthlong spooky season pop-up might help turn that around. 

“It’s about extending the season and having a good time,” Boehm says. “It’s not about having a Halloween day—it’s about having a Halloween season, like we did with Miracle.”

Halloween Every Day?

Of course, many bars trick out for Halloween independent of either franchise. And a committed handful celebrate the macabre all year round, such as NYC’s Paradise Lost, Los Angeles’s Beetle House, and spots like Vampire Café or The Crypt in New Orleans, a city that proudly boasts dozens of haunted and/or gothic bars, regardless of the season. 

But perhaps the longest-running year-round stalwart is Jekyl and Hyde, a Pittsburgh bar marking its 30th anniversary in 2026. (Its Instagram tagline reads, “Celebrating Halloween every day.”)

The space started as a typical neighborhood spot near East Carson Street, a main drag in the South Side neighborhood noted for its high concentration of bars, recalls owner Mike Alberter. When a regular customer who was in the business of building haunted houses offered to donate ghostly trappings after the season wrapped, Alberter saw an opportunity to make his bar stand out. Year after year, he added more black lights, fake cobwebs, miniature skulls, and more.

“There’s stuff on the ceilings, the walls,” Alberter says. “We put little spider rings into the drinks. We have candy out every day, like trick or treat.” 

While the two weeks leading up to Halloween are always packed, he says, business is steady all year long. Events like horror film screenings and “scary-oke” karaoke nights bring in costumed revelers eager to sip drinks including the signature Jac-O-Lantern (vanilla vodka, orange cream liqueur, orange juice, Sprite, and whipped cream).

“People love Halloween all year long [because] they love to dress up and be whoever,” he says. “I feel like Halloween is bigger than Christmas, in terms of money spent.”

Experiences and Escapism

Black Lagoon’s proprietors have opted to inject extra ghoulish glee into immersive events spanning beyond October. Hayes and Ramage also run Krampus Cove around the holidays, and recently expanded into the warmer months with their Summerween-inspired Bad Witch goth-girl pool parties. 

“People are looking for experiences more than anything,” Ramage observes. “Things are tough and heavy in terms of the world right now. The dollar is stretched. People want to go out and do more than just have drinks. People want to escape the world and enjoy some silly spookiness.”

Adding to that endeavor, mass merchandisers have steadily stretched the Halloween sales season earlier and earlier, erasing the gap between Summerween and All Hallow’s Eve. 

“We see Disney and Universal and the home décor stores are dropping their décor August 1,” Ramage says. That’s not necessarily a bad thing, either. “Halloween isn’t just October 31,” she says. “You can have Halloween vibes anytime.”

title: The World’s Largest Wine Cellar Is a 124-Mile-Long Treasure Trove
summary:
Far from a traditional wine cellar, the storage complex at Mileștii Mici in Moldova feels like an underground city.

The post The World’s Largest Wine Cellar Is a 124-Mile-Long Treasure Trove appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
It is a warm June day in Moldova when I arrive at Mileștii Mici, home to the largest cellar complex in the world. Situated among lush green landscapes in a town of the same name, the winery is a roughly 45-minute drive from the capital Chisinau and an hour and a half from the border with Ukraine. 

Its collection made the Guinness Book of World Records in 2007, when the cellars held about 1.5 million bottles; the stock count lasted several months. Even at Mileștii Mici, no one knows the exact current number, but estimates go up to 2 million. (I imagine a stock count now could take a year.)

A small electric train transports me through dark, subterranean surroundings until I am about 260 feet below ground—that’s at least 20 stories into the earth. It’s chilly down here, so I put on a jacket as I study the bottles around me. In the dim light, the oldest one I spot is from 1969. But soon it dawns on me that a great chunk of them come from one particular year: 1986.

Pedro, my guide, explains that it’s because of Mikhail Gorbachev. The last leader of the Soviet Union was convinced that his people drank too much, and so in 1986 he introduced strict rules that limited the purchase and sale of alcohol. Gorbachev’s “dry law” introduced quotas and rationing that led to overproduction relative to consumption. This era lasted around four years, Pedro says, and Soviets were limited to buying a few bottles per month per person. 

During this time, authorities destroyed wine supplies throughout the Soviet Union, of which Moldova was still a part. Fearful for their own stores, the owners of Mileștii Mici (founded in 1969, go figure) built secret rooms underground to protect their most rare and expensive bottles. There’s an irony there somewhere that Gorbachev could not have predicted: His prohibition led to an abundance of wine, a treasure trove of 1.5 million bottles or more, that has outlasted even him.

A Charming Hodgepodge of Wine and History

To say that the wine cellar at Mileștii Mici is enormous would be an understatement. The total length of the galleries is 200 kilometers (about 124 miles), of which about 55 kilometers (about 34 miles) are currently in use. The place was originally a limestone mine, in operation since 1886, and converted into a wine cellar in the late 1960s. Aesthetically, it’s all a bit of a charming hodgepodge: some sections have designs that gesture to old feudal castles, others to ancient Greek temples. 

Far from a traditional wine cellar, the storage complex at Mileștii Mici feels like an underground city, one through which you can actually drive your car. The scale of the place is massive, as are the thousands of oak barrels. Made in the 1970s and ’80s using wood imported from what is now Ukraine and Russia, the barrels have capacities that range from 600 to 2,000 wine decaliters.

Moldova’s wine culture is deeply rooted in the country’s history and identity, yet many international visitors know very little about it. One cannot find a better introduction to Moldovan wines than a visit to the Mileștii Mici wine cellar—or rather, city. 

At the end of the tour, guests can enjoy a glass or two of Moldovan wines accompanied with nibbles served in elegant tasting halls. On my visit, I indulge in a delicious plate of prosciutto crudo, salami, carpaccio, breadsticks, mixed nuts, and figs served with a young 2024 Chardonnay and a 2021 Cabernet Sauvignon. Sometimes, I’m told, these tastings even have live music played by Moldovan musicians.

Mileștii Mici has found creative ways to make use of all that space in the cellars, one of which is a regular race. 

First introduced in 2019, the Mileștii Mici Wineruns has participants running a total length of 10 kilometers (6 miles), part of it in the legendary galleries. According to Anton Zaharov, one of about 500 runners at a recent event, the dashing through those wine-filled stores is novel and unusual, but gets old real quick. 

“Most of the time you’re running through a dark, dimly lit tunnel of dust and sand,” he says. “Only the last two kilometers take you through the winery’s beautiful grounds.” One wine enthusiast’s paradise is one marathoner’s purgatory, it seems. At least they stay cool down there.

title: Is This Appellation the Last Great Wine Secret in France?
summary:
Château-Chalon, the iconic wine from an eponymous appellation in France’s Jura, offers drinkers something singular.

The post Is This Appellation the Last Great Wine Secret in France? appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Before you take your first sip of Château-Chalon, the iconic wine from an eponymous appellation in France’s Jura, it has already experienced several lifetimes. 

Each glass of the oxidative white wine rests for more than six years beneath a fragile veil of native yeast. The barrels are never topped up, leaving time, oxygen, and nature to slowly shape the Savagnin into something unmistakable. Even then, the story is unfinished. The bottles continue to evolve for years, often decades.

Perched high on a limestone escarpment in the Jura, Château-Chalon is a tiny appellation. Producers make only one wine in a distinctive style. Perhaps nowhere in France is the idea of terroir expressed with greater conviction.

Is it the country’s last great wine secret?

Terroir, Tradition, and the Intangible

People often point to Château-Chalon’s famous blue-grey marls as the source of its singularity. Formed beneath an ancient sea millions of years ago, these soils blanket the slopes and provide the slow, even conditions in which Savagnin thrives. 

Michel Campy, a geologist who has spent decades studying these hills, gently dismantles the myth: “Château-Chalon is not a unique terroir, despite what is constantly said.”

Similar marls throughout the Jura, he says. Soil alone cannot explain why this tiny village has produced one of France’s most distinctive wines for centuries.

Instead, Campy points to something less tangible.

“The quality of Château-Chalon comes from the fact that it is a terroir that has been worked for a very long time, with winegrowers committed to quality for centuries,” he says. “Little by little, Vin Jaune earned its reputation through human effort.”

It’s a holistic definition of terroir. Place matters, certainly, but so does memory. So does tradition. And so do generations of growers who have learned, vintage after vintage, how to read a landscape and resist the temptation to change it. 

In Château-Chalon, that philosophy reaches into every cellar.

“These wines are made by time and nature and of course by the winemaker as well,” explains Carmen Macle of Domaine Macle. “But time is very, very important for Château-Chalon. You need to let it age… otherwise the wine is not complete.”

There is perhaps no better description of Vin Jaune. The winemaker is present, but never dominant. The wine belongs first to time.

Patience has defined Château-Chalon for centuries. Long before 1936, when the appellation became one of France’s first AOCs, a nearby abbey shaped life in the vineyards. The abbesses decided when the harvest could begin and reserved the finest wines for religious purposes. In the ensuing decades, through phylloxera, harsh winters, and changing fashions, people in the village built a global reputation for their wines but never abandoned their slow, steady rhythms.

Facing the Future with Savoir-Faire

Today, however, that patience faces new challenges. Warmer vintages make balanced Savagnin increasingly difficult to produce, and the delicate veil of yeast that protects the wine during its long aging period is harder to maintain. “It’s difficult to have a veil of natural yeasts when you have a lot of alcohol and not enough acidity,” Macle says.

Despite these hurdles, winemakers are committed to upholding their generations-old heritage. 

“Château-Chalon is nothing without its history and savoir-faire,” Macle says. “We would change the essence of the wine if we changed something.”

With this steadfast commitment to tradition and identity, Château-Chalon has remained one of France’s last great wine secrets. Its oxidative style can be misunderstood, mistaken for a flaw rather than one of the world’s most extraordinary expressions of age and place. For Macle, that obscurity has been both a curse and a blessing. The wines remain rare, sought out by those willing to understand them rather than simply drink them.

There are more famous wines in France. More expensive ones, too. But few ask so much of everyone involved. The grower must trust generations of inherited knowledge. The winemaker must surrender to time. The drinker must learn to recalibrate their expectations.

Perhaps that is what makes Château-Chalon feel so singular today. It has survived by refusing to forget. Beneath its ancient marls, in the silence of its cellars, time still speaks with the loudest voice.

title: 9 of the World’s Best Wine Regions for Cycling
summary:
From Tuscany’s gravel roads to South Africa’s mountain passes, these wine regions reward cyclists with scenic rides and fantastic bottles.

The post 9 of the World’s Best Wine Regions for Cycling appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
It’s no wonder travelers are increasingly combining serious cycling and wine. The same geographic attributes that make for exhilarating pedaling—steep hills, sweeping vistas, and landscape diversity—also define some of the world’s most acclaimed wine regions.

“Our Porto to Lisbon cycling trip has seen bookings increase 31% year over year, while our Lisbon to Algarve trip is also seeing growth, with bookings up 40%,” says Katy Rockett, regional director of North America at tour operator Explore Worldwide. “Traveling by bike puts you directly into the landscape, riding through vineyards, agricultural areas, villages, and smaller communities, so there’s a much stronger connection between the wine you’re tasting and the place it comes from.”

“Pairing cycling with wine tourism answers a growing demand for immersive, active experiences,” adds Dagmar Lombard, general manager of Hôtel Crillon le Brave in southeastern France. “The rise of the electric bike has made it far more accessible – both for exploring the vineyards around us and for taking on a challenge like the ascent of Mont Ventoux.”

From the hilltop villages of Provence to the coastal trails of South Africa’s Stellenbosch, these are nine of the best wine regions to enjoy world-class cycling. 

Provence, France

Bike through fragrant lavender fields, hilltop villages, and ancient Roman roads in the bucolic hills of southeastern France. Grueling Mount Ventoux, an occasional host to the Tour de France, offers a challenging climb culminating in sprawling views of the Rhône Valley. Apart from its storied reputation, cyclists are drawn to the mountain’s moon-like summit, with its otherworldly expanse of white limestone. In its foothills, Hôtel Crillon le Brave inhabits the site of a 17th-century village and caters to cyclists with on-site equipment, rental deliveries, secure storage, and a full spa for soothing muscles post-pedal. The property is certified Accueil Vélo, France’s national designation for cycle-friendly businesses. Of course, the wine flows in Provence, cherished for its fresh, mineral-tinged rosés.

Douro Valley, Portugal 

The steep hillsides of this UNESCO World Heritage Site couple challenging terrain with dramatic scenery. Vines are planted along plunging slopes that border the Douro River, home to Port and quality DOC table wines. This is a destination for cyclists who are ready to sweat, with constant climbs and descents beside the terraced vineyards that cling to the valley’s schist-cut slopes. Adventurous spirits are rewarded with sweeping views of the storied valley and renowned selections at the area’s countless historic wine estates, known as quintas. Symington Family Estates runs some of the most famous, including Quinta do Vesúvio, which claims 800-plus acres in the Upper Douro Valley and dates back to the 16th century. With coveted vintage Ports and increasingly acclaimed dry table wines, this grand destination provides a fitting proverbial carrot during punishing gradients. 

Stellenbosch and Franschhoek, South Africa

In the Cape Winelands of South Africa, a thriving outdoor-adventure community makes the mountainous coastal landscape its playground. Stellenbosch offers cyclists their pick between road, gravel, and hundreds of miles of mountain bike trails. Pedal the Helshoogte Pass through the Simonsberg Mountains to Franschhoek, where you’ll find more leisurely routes on smooth, vineyard-lined lanes. There are several wine estates to visit on the way, including Delaire Graff, which offers suites and villas with private pool terraces and floor-to-ceiling windows for savoring mountain vistas. Once you’ve made your way to Franschhoek, the breathtaking Boekenhoutskloof is a historic winery where you can taste some of the region’s best Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, and Semillon.

Sonoma Valley, United States 

With 19 distinct AVAs spread among mountainsides, coastal trails, vibrant valleys, and redwood forests, Sonoma is a diverse getaway for wine lovers and cyclists alike. (Not that it’s a competition, but the Northern California region is larger and claims more bike-friendly roads than its neighbor, Napa.) Both casual and advanced riders will find a well-positioned base in the Healdsburg and Dry Creek Valley area in North Sonoma. Quiet roads wind up and down gentle hills, passing over a dozen wineries on the roughly 10-mile West Dry Creek Road. Stop for lunch at Lambert Bridge for a picnic basket stuffed with local cheeses and charcuterie, best enjoyed in the winery’s pristine gardens. Riesling fans should also break to sample the trio at Reeve Wines. For an extended journey that delves into challenging terrain, venture into the adjacent valleys of Alexander Valley and Russian River Valley or the Mayacamas Mountains.  

Loire Valley, France

Central France has much to offer the epicurean outdoor adventurer. The 560-mile trail known as La Loire à Vélo, or Loire Valley by Bike, starts in Cuffy, a small village in Burgundy, and winds towards the Atlantic Coast at Saint-Brevin-les-Pins, passing Renaissance châteaux, quaint riverside villages, and world-class vineyards. Take the Via Allier south of the official Loire à Vélo to reach the singular Côtes d’Auvergne AOC, where vines and bike routes share the same volcanic hillsides. Known for its Gamay and Pinot Noir reds and rosés, like those from fifth-generation producer Desprat Saint Verny, the AOC offers a rare chance to pair cycling through volcanic landscapes with a distinctive wine culture that dates back to Roman times.  

Barossa Valley, Australia

Perfect for casual riders and serious oenophiles, the Barossa Trail is a 25-mile sealed cycling and walking path weaving through the heart of Australian wine country. Gentle gradients make for easy pedaling, while public restrooms and water stations keep breaks convenient. Of course, no journey is complete without plenty of pit stops at cellar doors, cafes, and farm stands. Take the connecting Gomersal Trail from Lyndoch to visit Seppeltsfield Wines, the makers of a 100-point red blend that blew away Wine Enthusiast Writer-at-Large Christina Pickard. The sealed detour traverses local farm roads under vast Australian skies, leading to an expansive, palm-lined winery complex with a rich history.

Girona and the Empordá, Spain

Girona has earned an international reputation as a cycling hub, but the roads surrounding the Catalan city also lead to one of Spain’s most distinctive wine regions. In DO Empordá, cyclists can ride through cork forests, medieval villages, and sea vistas before stopping for tastings of Garnatxa Negra and Carinyena, the region’s signature grapes. Road cyclists tackle the region’s rolling secondary roads, while gravel riders have extensive unpaved terrain to explore, including sections of the 217-mile Pirinexus loop. The official DO Empordà Wine Route includes over thirty wineries, and it can be followed on two wheels. For a particularly scenic ride, take the route toward Cap de Creus, where vineyards stretch from the Mediterranean to the foothills of the Pyrenees.

Willamette Valley, United States 

Oregon’s Willamette Valley Scenic Bikeway is the perfect two-to-three-day cycling adventure punctuated by farm stands, waterfalls, and Pinot Noir tastings. The nation’s first official Scenic Bikeway covers 134 miles of agricultural landscape, winding through the fertile valley between the Coast and Cascade ranges. It runs directly past Ankeny Vineyard, where cyclists can stop to sample Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, and wood-fired pizza. Elsewhere, the mostly gentle ride follows quiet country roads past hop fields, hazelnut orchards, Christmas tree farms, and the Willamette River, with plenty of refueling options along the way. 

Tuscany, Italy

For red wine lovers, no destination tops Tuscany’s storied winemaking history and diversity of bottles, all set against the backdrop of its famous rolling hills. But cycling is nearly as ingrained in Tuscan culture as its world-renowned Sangiovese. Cyclists flock to its white gravel roads lined with cypress trees, relishing scenic rides through medieval towns, olive groves, and vineyards. There are options for every type of athlete among its 9,000-plus miles of routes, from peaceful paths along the centuries-old Via Francigena to the famously arduous climb from Castelnuovo di Garfagnana to San Pellegrino. And with celebrated wine regions like Chianti Classico and Montalcino woven into the landscape, cyclists can easily pair a day in the saddle with a well-earned tasting.

content:
High Praise for Loire Wines:

France’s Answer to Sustainable, Crowd-Pleasing Bottles Perfect for Any Occasion

 

Few viticultural areas reflect such innate diversity—as well as a commitment to sustainability—as France’s Loire region. Located south west of Paris, this dynamic wine-growing area is home to a mosaic of soil types and grape varieties, which lead to a versatile lineup of wine styles and flavor profiles. From the coastal Nantais vineyards to the central Anjou-Saumur and Touraine sub-regions, Loire Wines comprises 34 appellations and denominations across 42,000 hectares of vines, meaning there’s a perfectly suited Loire wine for every palate—it’s simply a matter of knowing where to look.

Year after year, the quality of Loire wines continues to capture the attention of industry professionals, and the proof is in the bottles. After a recent tasting panel, Loire wines garnered show-stopping scores across a variety of categories and styles, further affirming the region’s place as a world-class viticultural zone.

Curious to learn more? Wine Enthusiast recently rated a lineup of Loire Wines crafted from different grape varieties in various styles. Our standout selections are highlighted below.

Click Here to Download Our 2026 Loire Wine Ratings

Captivating Whites That Go the Limits

White wines garnered impressive scores across a number of Loire appellations, including Saumur, Touraine Chenonceaux, and Muscadet Sèvre et Maine Clisson, further cementing the demand for refreshing, easy-drinking white wines. From the Atlantic coast, Famille Lieubeau Muscadet Sèvre-et-Maine Clisson 2023 (WE Best Buy, 94 points) enchanted tasters with its vibrant acidity and saline undertones, while Domaine La Rochette Touraine 2023 (WE Editors’ Choice, 92 points) offered an invigorating take on Sauvignon Blanc marked by flinty undertones and a long finish.

Further inland, the versatility of Chenin Blanc also showed promising results. From Saumur, Domaine de Rocheville Côte de Parnay 2023 (92 points) highlighted the complexity and distinct minerality of Chenin grown on tuffeau and clay-limestone soils, while Château de Fesles 2015 (WE Editors’ Choice, 95 points) from Bonnezeaux spoke to the cellar-worthy potential of well-crafted Chenin. Lastly, Vignoble Alain Robert Les Charmes 2024 (92 points) beautifully depicted the essence of Vouvray with its juicy orchard fruit notes and zippy acidity.

Top Scoring Reds for Every Occasion

Like Loire whites, the high scores achieved by the region’s red wines spoke to the increasingly growing demand for lively, food-friendly expressions that can be enjoyed with or without food. Within the Loire, the Cabernet Franc, Pinot Noir, and Gamay varieties offer a tried-and-true solution, especially when enjoyed with a slight chill. From Bourgueil, Yannick Amirault Le Grand Clos 2023 (WE Editors’ Choice, 93 points), made from organically-farmed old vines, charmed with its elegance, freshness, and structural integrity. Likewise, Clotilde Legrand Les Rogelins 2011 (WE Editors’ Choice, 95 points), showcased the grape’s remarkable ability to withstand long bouts of aging, thanks to its structured acidity and well-integrated tannins.

Elsewhere in Touraine, Domaine Jacky Marteau Touraine Gamay 2025 (WE Best Buy, 91 points) showed the Loire’s unique take on the grape—one that highlights bright red fruit flavors, vivacious acidity, and pleasantly peppery undertones. Similarly, Pinot Noir lovers will take delight in La Fille Couillaud Bernier 2023 (WE Best Buy, 91 points), a smooth and silky bottling with notes of cherry, strawberry, and damp earth. These smooth and easy-drinking reds are ideal for casually enjoying with friends or pairing with a variety of dishes, especially if grilled meats, mushrooms, or tomato-based sauces are on the menu.

Sparkling Wines That Shine

In addition to high-scoring still wines, the Loire also produces a diverse array of sparkling bottlings that rival the world’s best. The area is France’s largest producer of appellation-designated sparkling wines after Champagne, and utilizes the same production method to create its signature bubbles to craft refreshing white and savory rosé expressions. title: The Largest Wine Cellar in Switzerland Sits Inside a Luxe Wellness Hotel
summary:
Appenzeller Huus, an alpine retreat in the Swiss town of Gonten, houses a multi-room wine cellar with over 18,000 bottles.

The post The Largest Wine Cellar in Switzerland Sits Inside a Luxe Wellness Hotel appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
In the corner of northeast Switzerland, an hour’s drive away from Zurich, the Appenzell region is home to many charming curiosities: its own distinct regional variety of Swiss German, an annual cattle parade where farmers lead a herd through town while wearing enormous cowbells, and a health-focused resort with the largest wine cellar in the country. 

It belongs to Appenzeller Huus, an alpine retreat in the town of Gonten (population: 1,477) with three distinct hotel concepts: the luxury wellness hotel Huus Quell; the design-forward boutique stay Huus Löwen; and the cozy inn Huus Bären that dates back to 1602.

Among the retreat’s holdings is a massive multi-room wine cellar with a label count in the thousands and a bottle count in the five figures. It’s an oenophile’s treasure trove rendered in glass and stone. And as for the guests at the resort in search of a little detox: well, a little wine never hurt anyone. 

The Design

The wine cellar at Appenzeller Huus is a series of four rooms with varying designs, each designed to house specific types of wine. The first three are dedicated to red wines, white wines, and Champagnes, all stored in purpose-built glass cellars underneath Huus Quell that surround the Barrel Room. It is exactly what it’s called—a room shaped like a barrel, where bottles on glass shelves line the perimeter. This beautifully modern and intimate space functions as a private dining area for nine people. 

Guests who book the Barrel Room can elect to have an eight-course dinner with meticulously paired wines prepared solely for their party. Wines made in Switzerland are the star of a fourth room, installed in Huus Bären’s original cellar, a stone cave over 100 years old.

Equipped with the latest wine storage and security features, all the cellars utilize keyless retinal scanning for entry.

The Collection

Within these impressive cellars are 18,000 bottles representing 2,160 wines. The whole operation is overseen by cellar master Hans Rhyner, a former railroad worker who first sated his curiosity about wine by doing it the old fashioned way: He simply bought wines and tried them. Self-taught and passionate, Rhyner oversaw the wine program at Michelin-recognized Hotel Dorfhus Gupf, located in Rehetobel, about a half-hour away by car from Appenzeller Huus. 

At the Dorfhus, he was recognized for seeking out small, creative wineries, especially those led by female winemakers. Asked about this attention well paid, Rhyner says that women have more compassion and care for their vineyards.

To manage the 18,000-bottle collection, the wine cellar at Appenzeller Huus uses a computerized database that tracks everything in the four cellars by label, style, grapes, producer, vineyard, and other arcane details.  

What Makes It Special

Apart from the novelty of such a monumental cellar located in small-town Switzerland, one of the most special qualities of the wine cellar at Appenzeller Huus is the obvious dedication to small and independent producers. Rhyner’s love of excellent craftsmanship—whether in the bottle or in the cellars that house them—is evident. 

As for the cellar’s home in Appenzeller Huus, that can be attributed to another oenophile: the resort’s owner Jan Shoch, the former CEO of Leonteq, a Swiss financial technology and services company. He developed Appenzeller Huus after buying a hotel in which his parents honeymooned—the hotel that is now Huus Bären. The wine cellar is essential, he says, to Huus Quell.

To him, there’s a sense of wellness that comes from the pleasure of taking time to savor something truly special, be it a quiet moment with the natural landscapes of Switzerland or a glass of wine. Here, you get both.

Why Dual Zone Just Makes Sense

The Right Temperature for Every Bottle

Proper storage temperature is the key to bringing out the best in every bottle. While both reds and whites can be stored long-term at 53–57°F, their ideal serving temperatures are another story. Whites and other light wines should be served cooler (45–52°F), while reds require warmer temperatures (58–65°F) to fully express their character.

Unlike single-zone wine coolers, which keep a uniform temperature throughout and are best for aging or storing just one variety, dual-zone wine coolers feature two independently controlled climate zones. This makes them the ultimate solution for those who want to keep both reds and whites perfectly stored and ready to enjoy on the regular.

Less Thinking, More Sipping

With separate temperature controls, you can keep your whites crisp and your reds right where you want them. So instead of planning ahead for which bottle you want, you can simply choose what you’re in the mood for and enjoy.

title: Wine Should Be About Slowing Down. Latinos Have a Word for That
summary:
Perhaps the wine world has forgotten what a good bottle is meant to do: bring people together.

The post Wine Should Be About Slowing Down. Latinos Have a Word for That appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
When I was growing up, there was rarely a clean ending to dinner and family gatherings. A meal might technically be over, but nobody would get up. Someone would make coffee and put sugar on the table, another would pour drinks. The stories would get louder and more repetitive in the way family stories do. That’s at least how it goes in mine—folks from Southern Tennessee and Mexicans from Texas. All I knew was that, well past dessert, everyone was just happy to stay.

We never called that ritual sobremesa. But I’ve started hearing it used more often when talking about wine, most recently at a dinner in Los Angeles built around the tradition, hosted by Andrea Jaramillo of Más Vino Please.

From the Spanish “sobre” meaning over, above, or after, and “mesa,” the word for table, sobremesa refers to the stretch of time after a meal when everyone remains at the table, talking, drinking, laughing, and generally showing no urgency about whatever comes next. The term is used across parts of Latin America and Spain, though customs and exact language vary widely. I wouldn’t retroactively call every long epilogue to the family meals of my Mexican American childhood “sobremesa.” We didn’t. The instinct behind it? Completely familiar.

That familiarity extends far beyond my own family. The 2025 World Happiness Report, which looked at Gallup data from 142 countries and territories, reports that residents in Latin America and the Caribbean ate roughly nine lunches and dinners with other people each week. Those who shared more meals also reported greater life satisfaction and more positive emotions. Researchers found that this association was comparable in strength to factors like income and unemployment.

There’s a pretty stark American counterpoint. In 2023, 26% of adults in the United States said they had eaten every meal alone the previous day, a 53% increase from 2003. The trend showed up across all age groups, with particularly sharp recent increases among younger adults—the same adults who report higher levels of loneliness. So maybe what I remember isn’t simply a charming family habit, and there’s something meaningful about staying at the table. 

Lately I’ve been wondering whether that instinct, that sense of sobremesa, is something the wine world has forgotten. In the past few years, the wine industry has constantly struggled to get younger people to drink more wine. According to 2025 Wine Market Council data, 39% of infrequent wine drinkers cited health concerns, but a greater 43% said that wine often does not fit the settings in which they drink. Put simply: the vibe of wine, for them, isn’t right. 

That number stuck with me because wine spends a lot of time trying to cultivate a sense of occasion. There are tastings and pairing dinners, flights and master classes, special bottles saved for special meals. It can all be overwhelming. Even casual wine drinking can come with homework: Is this the right glass to use? Should this be chilled? What am I supposed to taste? Am I supposed to know where this tiny French village is? Wine may be one of the only drinks people regularly apologize for not knowing enough about before ordering it. 

Sobremesa works almost in reverse. The occasion isn’t the bottle, but that nobody is ready to leave. That idea is familiar to David Salazar, founder and winemaker of Reclamación Wines. In his Mexican American family, he says, gathering around the table was about much more than food.

“It was how we stayed connected and held on to our culture,” Salazar says. “It was where I heard my parents and their friends tell stories about everything from their childhood and adolescence in Mexico to coming to the United States.” 

Those stories were funny, sad, and sometimes scary, he recalls, and after dinner came the inevitable botana—chicharrón, cacahuates, or cueritos—with a few drinks still on the table. “The drinks were part of the gathering, but they were never the focus,” Salazar says. “They simply gave us another reason to stay at the table a little longer.”

That last part feels especially relevant to wine right now. Salazar thinks the industry has made the experience of drinking and enjoying wine harder than it needs to be. “Wine culture has been its own worst enemy,” he says. “For years, winemakers, sommeliers, tasting room staff, and even self-proclaimed ‘knowledgeable consumers’ have made wine feel intimidating, almost like a test people can fail.” 

The result, he says, is a culture that can feel like a “cool kids club” to people on the outside. “We’ve spent years making people feel like they need the right vocabulary, palate, glassware, and knowledge before they’re allowed to enjoy wine, and then we act surprised when they choose something else,” he says. “No one wants to spend money on something that makes them feel stupid.”

That disconnect matters when an industry is trying to court people who don’t already consider themselves “wine people.” Maybe the goal shouldn’t be turning everybody into one. There’s a difference between helping people understand what they’re drinking and making them feel like understanding it is a prerequisite for enjoying it. 

In the meals I grew up around, nobody needed to identify cassis or graphite before pouring another glass. A drink existed alongside food, gossip, teasing, family stories, and the same anecdotes everyone had already heard 50 times. A bottle of red might be on the table next to a bottle of brown liquor next to whatever beer somebody had brought. Drinking the wine—or anything at the table—didn’t require performing expertise. It was simply about participating in the evening, in extending a moment of togetherness. 

Salazar sees the same distinction in the gatherings he grew up around, where nobody discussed things like, say, beer production methods. Lagers and ales can reach similar levels of craft and complexity as wine, but most people never worry about knowing everything there is to know about an IPA. “Understanding its complexity wasn’t a prerequisite for enjoying it,” he says. “It was a catalyst for connection rather than exclusion.”

That’s also what clicked for me at that sobremesa-inspired dinner in Los Angeles. Rather than a formal tasting built around analyzing one bottle after another, the night was loose: shared plates, conversation, and red wine served without much ceremony. Campo Viejo was the wine partner, but what stayed with me wasn’t a particular bottle or cocktail. It was that the wine never seemed to demand everyone to stop talking and pay attention to it. It was just there, doing what wine arguably does best: giving people another reason to linger.

“Sobremesa is all about connection,” Jaramillo says. “Connecting with the people we love or meeting someone new.” And connection, she points out, takes time—the kind spent talking, learning about each other, and being intentional about staying present. Wine can fit naturally into that rhythm. 

“Many times, sobremesa moments are anchored by a bottle of wine,” Jaramillo says. “It’s the reason we linger at the table a little longer and slowly finish the evening.” That was also the intention behind the dinner, she explains, where the only thing on the agenda was “a slower pace.”

None of this is to suggest that the wine industry should take a cultural tradition, turn it into a marketing concept, and call the youth problem solved. That would miss the point spectacularly. Sobremesa isn’t a consumer-acquisition strategy. It’s a way of thinking about what eating and drinking are actually for. Connection comes first. The drink fits into it.

For years, wine has tried to teach people how to drink wine. I didn’t grow up learning how to taste it. I grew up learning how to stay, how to connect, how to be a person people want to be around. And then I got interested in what we were drinking. Maybe wine could use a little more of that. Salazar carries that philosophy into his own wines, telling people there is no right or wrong way to drink them. Red Solo cup? Fine. Nice stemware? Also fine. As he puts it, “If you’re drinking wine, you’re doing it right.”

title: What’s Really Going On with Restaurant Wine Pricing?
summary:
Wine director Michael Laudenslager and importer Peter Andrews join the WE Podcast to discuss how restaurant wine pricing became so expensive.

The post What’s Really Going On with Restaurant Wine Pricing? appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
You’re at a restaurant, scanning the wine list, and you see by-the-glass options priced at $17, $20, and $23. The inevitable question hits you: To Google or not to Google? Is it better to see how much these bottles cost at retail, exposing the grim realities of restaurant markups? Or is ignorance bliss, especially during a night out?

Restaurant by-the-glass prices used to generally align with the bottles’ wholesale costs, but that’s no longer the case. As the price for a glass of wine creeps higher and higher, we’re left wondering… why? Sure, drinking wine at restaurants has always been a little luxurious, but now it seems even more inaccessible to the average diner.

Clearly, I had questions about what’s happening behind the scenes, so to help me find answers, I invited a sommelier and an importer to join me on the Wine Enthusiast Podcast. Michael Laudenslager is a Wine Enthusiast writer-at-large who reviews Italian wines from the sub-regions of Tuscany, Southern Italy, and Sardinia. He’s a sommelier with many years of hospitality experience and is currently the wine director at Peasant in New York City.

Peter Andrews is the founder of Culture Wine Co., an importer, wholesaler, and e-comm retailer focused on South African wines. Based in San Francisco, Peter is also the co-creator of Hella Chenin, an annual wine festival that celebrates the many joys of Chenin Blanc. (Look for Peter on our 2026 Rising Stars list.)

A quick disclaimer: Wine Enthusiast loves restaurants! We love drinking wine at them and the people who run them, and we are in no way trying to denigrate restaurants, where profit margins have always been thin. But still, why are by-the-glass prices so high?

On the Reason Why BTG Markups Seem So High

Michael Laudenslager: “Being in New York City, I think people are just really trying to take advantage. This is probably like the first part of the answer—people are really trying to take advantage of high pricing again. I’m so sick and tired of talking about Covid. It’s been so long now, but there are some ripple effects, for sure, that we’re feeling. But we are feeling, not just the city, but the world, coming back to life in terms of not being so price-conscious of things anymore. In New York, there’s some ultra-premium pricing on by-the-glass, man. And I personally hate it, because I know the price of 90% of the bottles that I’m picking to drink. So in my head I’m costing things out, and I’m like, ‘Damn, they’re really bopping me over the head for this glass of Burgundy.’”

Peter Andrews: “Rents have gone out of control, food costs are out of control, and labor costs are extremely high. And not that people don’t deserve to be paid more, but restaurants run on incredibly thin margins. And those three things adding up make it extremely hard to run a restaurant. Wine and alcohol in general have always been, kind of, the safety net to allow you to make any extra margin to cover all of those low-margin categories, so it makes sense that they need to be marked up so high. But I think we’re kind of at this point now where consumers are saying, ‘Enough is enough. I’m not paying this amount for wine anymore. I don’t value it this much anymore. I don’t understand why I should pay $20 or more for a glass. And so, I’m gonna go to a cocktail or a mocktail or, god forbid, an RTD at a restaurant.’”

On the Balancing Act Between Premiumization and Attracting New Customers

PA: “The more I expand into other markets, I’m seeing that even $15 is kind of the peak for a lot of markets. So, I’m in this really interesting Catch-22 because my entire business model is trying to premiumize South African wine and get them viewed as the world-class quality that they are. And the more that you discount or position something as ‘value,’ the more you lower the ceiling of its potential. The reality is, you need to give customers and consumers a good price point to actually jump in. But the other end of it is, you don’t want to diminish its ability to be viewed as a premium product. So we’re in a really precarious time right now as an entire industry figuring out how to get people to drink more.”

Check Out Our YouTube Channel

On the Psychology of Wine Pricing

ML: “Especially if it’s a grape that people don’t know… $20 scares people. $19 doesn’t. I’m not saying a hundred percent of the time, but if you want to sell more wine, there’s so much psychology behind it. People go in there saying, ‘I don’t want to spend $100 for a bottle of wine.’ But if you put it at $90, now you could probably get a little upsell going from someone who wanted to spend $80 on a bottle. But taking them to $100 is a little difficult.

I think we have to pick and choose what we want to do with the beverage cost. And that could be for a $25 glass of wine: Go backwards—charge $22. Now you’re gonna get people thinking about what they might spend for a glass of wine. But psychology is a big part of it from what I have seen in my career in creating beverage programs.”

On the Key to Wine’s Future Success

PA: “This can go in a million ways, but the beauty is that wine has never been better. There’s phenomenal wine made in every country in the world. And so it’s really about if we can do our job as importers, distributors, restaurateurs, retailers, as an industry, to bring curiosity back into the equation. The future is super bright. Wine opens the doors to discovery and learning about history, about language, about culture, about food. You get to travel around the world and meet interesting people that you otherwise probably wouldn’t have met. We should be yelling this from the rooftops, everywhere possible. And the more that we can get that out, the more consumers and trade, who are gatekeepers, are going to be interested in trying and exploring new places. Life is just so damn expensive now that restaurants and retail shops are going to have to adapt with price points that are more reasonable, or they’ll perish.”

On the Lingering Effects of the Pandemic

PA: “I think we’ve seen a massive brain-drain in our industry since Covid. Many really high-powered salespeople and executives and operations people just left the industry altogether. And I think, even more important are the amount of servers who aren’t being captured into becoming wine lovers. That used to be, like, the number one pipeline for us. And it’s, anecdotally, pretty clear we’re not capturing those potentially budding wine professionals to stay in wine. So we have to realize that we’re kind of getting attacked from all sides. But I think, from a restaurant point of view, it’s not just staying alive, it’s not just selling more wine; it’s becoming a really good educator and someone who can inspire hopefully one or two servers to become sommeliers and grow in their wine journey.”

On What Makes a Great Wine List (and What Doesn’t)

ML: “Everybody wants to make the same wine list, and it drives me crazy. People can’t let go of Burgundy. People can’t let go of certain areas that just excite the sommelier, but they’re not looking at what’s around them. They’re not reading the room. They’re not seeing the program. They just want to have an amazing wine list with the best wines, and it kind of drives me crazy.

What I’m looking for right now… and I am having a hard time finding it in New York City, which should be, you know, probably easy to find, and should have some of the best wine programs in the world, which they do. However, I can’t find a 100% French program that’s exploring so many different regions and so many different varietals. I haven’t found a Languedoc section that could go deep. I haven’t found sections of France that I haven’t heard of that someone could really go in on and then say, ‘Yo, check these grapes out. I’ve never heard of them.’ And chances are, if you haven’t heard of the grape in that region, they’re probably gonna be pretty affordable or at least [have] more value. And that’s gonna help everyone. That’s gonna help the people importing that wine because if they’re not super popular, we’re not doing our job at trying to push those wines, and it doesn’t help explore the whole country of France… 

When does safe win in restaurants? You know what I mean? What great restaurants are safe? You know, unless it’s like a neighborhood spot that we love and enjoy—sure. And if once in a while I want to go to a shitty Italian restaurant and drink Chianti by the glass, I’m happy as hell. Or drink a Sauvignon Blanc at the airport that’s filled to the brim, I don’t care. However, we’re talking about good restaurants and great wine programs. I’m not saying everybody needs to follow the guidelines that we’re throwing out there right now, or the ideas that we’re going against, but the people that sit at the pretty good tier to the great tier, they should probably get in touch more with what they’re doing and what they’re selling. And that could be said like for any cuisine, whether it’s Portuguese, South African, France—really build a program that’s unique.”

The Guests

Michael Laudenslager reviews wines from subregions of Tuscany, Southern Italy, and Sardinia. He is the Wine Director at Respect Hospitality’s restaurant Peasant and a seasoned sommelier with certification from the Court of Master Sommeliers. His career includes managing the beverage programs for renowned chefs Marc Forgione, Peter McAndrew, and Tony Clark; serving as the Director of Restaurants for Marriott International in Washington, D.C. and New York; and curating and pouring wines at the original Smith & Wollensky in New York.

Peter Andrews is the founder of Culture Wine Co. and a 15-year industry veteran whose career spans wine retail, executive roles in the trade, and teaching for Johnson and Wales University, The Culinary Institute of America at Greystone, and Wine and Spirits Education Trust (WSET). He is the co-founder of Hella Chenin, the only Chenin Blanc-focused wine festival in the U.S., and Small Poppies Wine Collective, an importer group supporting underrepresented regions and small-scale producers.

I think the future is super bright. Like, wine opens the doors to discovery and learning about history, about language, about culture, about food. You get to travel around the world and meet interesting people that you otherwise probably wouldn’t have met. We should be yelling this from the rooftops, everywhere possible. And the more that we can get that out, the more consumers and trade who are gatekeepers are going to be interested in trying and exploring new places. So I think if the future can be so bright, if we can really lean into that, I think in the end, I don’t think we’re going to slow down in terms of things being extremely expensive. Life is just so damn expensive now that restaurants are going to have to, and retail shops are going to have to, adapt with price points that are more reasonable or they’ll perish. It’s just a fact.

There will be the 1% that crushes the three-Michelin stars, and any price point doesn’t matter to them. But the majority of people need price points that are reasonable for them. And the adaptation will be regions that have been otherwise underrepresented. So that’s just gonna make the table bigger. It’s going to make things more exciting. And I think the best wine directors and buyers at retail shops will lean into that, and they’ll be at the vanguard of that and they’ll be the ones who are the leaders of that kind of next wave. So I’m bullish on it. It’s just a matter of figuring out where your price thresholds are so that you can get more people partaking without obviously going into the red as a business.

RG

I think part of that’s a perception problem too. In the U.S., compared to most Western European countries, people think of wine as this luxury, this thing that should be sort of expensive, this thing that you might not always need at dinner, but you should have it, but that’s just what it costs. Whereas in other countries, and obviously there are huge economic issues at hand and it’s not apples to oranges comparing the U.S. to France or Spain or whatever, but I think some of that needs to shift too, right? I think the perception that especially younger people have needs to shift. But part of the problem is, they go to a restaurant in New York and they see that all the wines are twenty, twenty one, twenty-two dollars. And it’s tough for them to change their mind about it until these prices start to change.

PA

I also think we’ve seen a massive brain drain in our industry since COVID, whether it’s at the highest level, look at RNDC, you have to imagine when the dust settles there, we’ll see how many really high-powered salespeople and executives and operations people just left the industry altogether. And I think even more important are the amount of servers that aren’t being captured into becoming wine lovers.

And that used to be the number one pipeline for us. And it’s anecdotally pretty clear we’re not capturing those young or potentially budding wine professionals to stay in wine. So we have to realize that we’re kind of getting attacked from all sides. But I think from a restaurant point of view, it’s not just staying alive, it’s not just selling more wine. It’s becoming a really good educator and someone who can inspire hopefully one or two servers to become leads, to become sommeliers, to then grow in their wine journey. But that’s been a hard thing to capture, I think. 

And Michael, I don’t know if you’ve experienced this or see this, but I definitely see this on my side on the wholesale journey. I import wholesale, but my main job is pounding the pavement with a bag of wine to restaurants and retailers now around the country. And I see a lot of green buyers. I see a lot of sommeliers and wine directors that are also the ops director, the marketing person, the janitor, right? And like, how can they possibly be good at any of those jobs if they’ve got too much on their plate as well? 

So, it’s like we also have to look at figuring out how to support the wine professionals, but also keeping the budding ones in the wine world. Otherwise, they’re gonna go off in a different profession and we’re really gonna be struggling in five, 10 years time to have enough professionals to move the needle.

ML

Peter, I couldn’t agree with you more with the change after COVID. And again, I’ll keep saying it, I hate talking about COVID anymore, but it is real  what you’re saying. The beverage director role nearly became extinct, right? Because you had to eliminate positions and become a profitable place again. And I understand that. But after people left, and this happened all over the place: the best GMs, the best floor managers, the best wine directors kind of figured other things out and left their profession to go do other things, whether it’s a better work-life balance or just something that they found passion in or whatever. But what we found is all my buddies, myself included, we’re not just a wine director anymore and we just don’t focus on beverage. It doesn’t mean that you never worked the floor of the restaurant or the operation. But we became some of the top dogs that knew what the hell was going on in a restaurant. And we were the ones looked to to either run the operation, train new managers, or if something broke, we knew what to do because we were the ones probably in the restaurant industry the longest.

We had managers that weren’t in it for a long time. You know, a lot of kids moved into New York after COVID because pricing was correct and all these things were happening. So it was a little bit more attractive at the time. That’s not the story now. But we’d get a lot of green people in this industry, and we were the ones doing everything, from setting up private events to running the whole show like a GM would.

And at the same time running a beverage program. And you really cannot focus on your job or make it the best you can when all those things are happening. You know, I’m not saying it’s impossible, but that’s absolutely true. 

And the whole server aspect of it, I agree. I obviously don’t support drinking at work. That is not good, right? However, you should be tasting with your team, not just at pre-shift. If they’re opening up a bottle of wine, they should be tasting that wine. Looking at the label and you should be watching them do it, not a hundred percent of the time. But you know, be cognizant that that’s happening, and maybe run over and they could be busy, but if they’re opening up a bottle of Sangiovese and you make sure that they know it’s Sangiovese, then that should be happening, and then maybe later at the end of that shift if you have a by-the-glass example of that, go ahead and let them try it, and talk with them. But you can’t learn wine on paper, you know. You have to taste wine, and that’s it, man. You know, and the servers are are just like the guests. They have to know what’s the good stuff, and why we have it, why that’s unique and why I wanna sell it, so they should go through the same experience as the guests should. And it’s super, super important to get servers excited about this.

RG

Yeah, they’re on the front lines and, especially for people who are not going to bottle shops, they’re the key wine educators for so many consumers, even if it’s just a brief conversation about a glass.

Well, I think we’ve covered a lot of ground here. I’m not sure if we totally solved all the problems about the wine and restaurants. But to get back to education, I think that’s such a big topic and a whole other episode. Especially with new drinkers, people who see a price like that, it’s such a big part of it, on the somm, on the server, to really hype up a wine. Because twenty bucks is twenty bucks.

ML

I think another important thing is of course how we present wine. And before I say this, I am not really feeling a big decrease in wine sales or that people aren’t drinking wine. Of course, we have flip flop nights where it’s a heavy cocktail night. But at the end of the day, we are rocking it in selling wine. And I don’t know what the real answer is, or if there is a problem. But I do feel—and I don’t have stats or anything to support this argument—but I don’t think people are drinking less wine right now. I think they are drinking different wine, maybe different price points, or they’re exploring different avenues of wine. 

Maybe some producers are feeling hurt. Maybe some importers that have a really broad, mediocre portfolio are feeling hurt. Maybe Prosecco sales are down. You know, but if that’s the case, I support what’s happening. I’m sorry that we’re not selling as much cheap Prosecco. I’m sorry we’re not selling tons of the average Chianti, you know, whatever. But what I’m seeing is people are very interested in wine, and they’re exploring different avenues. And education definitely is important to help guide that whole process, because if we’re giving them different stuff, we have to know what we’re selling.

PA

Yeah, and I think that’s where importers and distributors come in, right? I think the future of our little tier is smaller and mightier. I think the majority of high-quality restaurants and retailers want to work with the big distributors as little as possible. And they want to curate, right? So they may be looking at smaller lists with less SKUs, but highly curated. So the concept of not being everything to everyone is probably the way forward, but it’s wines that like you’re behind every single one of them. And the way that works is working with more vendors. And so it’s up to us as importers, distributors, whether you’re one or both, to be highly specialized, highly educated, able to actually perform your task of selling and delivering the wine on time, which I know is still a big challenge with a lot of distributors.

And then showing up and being helpful with staff trainings. And I think you and the restaurant need to collaborate in a significant way for that. It’s easy to just fill the slot every Tuesday in a staff training, but really be intentional about it. And then it’s on the distributor and the importer to create demand. 

One of the things that I’m trying to do with Culture Wine Co. is to really grow a good social media presence. So then as I grow and I look at opening new accounts or great ones that are existing, I can say, “Well, hey, I’ve got 10,000 or 15,000 or whatever followers. Why don’t we do a collaborative post together about this badass wine pairing that you’re doing with one of my wines? And let’s drive some traffic to your establishment. Let’s partner together beyond just me being your order taker.” And I think that’s the ticket right now: buyers and wine directors understanding that there’s a partnership in the distributor and the importer that can be utilized in a very significant way. 

And again, that can come from education to programming. The sky’s the limit. I think the more that you can lean on your smaller distributor partners and importers to develop creative programming, the more you’re gonna see people partake in the wine program itself. So I love to hear from restaurants that they’re like, “Hey, we’re thinking about this. We want to do a volume deal on that. We want to have a staff training around these three places in South Africa.” I’m like, “Bring it on. I am so down to do all of this.” And in the end, that creates inspiration in the servers and in the young junior somms to stick with it, to sell it, and then to get that consumer that had one glass to maybe move up into the bottle. I think it all starts there.

RG

Absolutely. Well, I think we gotta wrap up here. Thank you so much for coming on, guys. This was great.

ML

Always good hanging with you.

RG

Yeah, good to see you. Thank you.

PA

Thank you very much.

ML

Alright, Peter, I’ll catch you later, man.

Letter from the Publisher

Ahead of the Trend

The best wine discoveries are the ones you find before everyone else catches on.

As a former indie-music snob and Pitchfork reader before it went corporate, I absolutely understand the thrill of getting in on the ground floor. There is something deeply satisfying about having your own little secret relationship with a band, a place, or a bottle of wine before the masses claim it as their own.

This is the space where our annual Top 100 Best Buys list shines.

Read More

There have never been more entry points into wine that overdeliver. From the Languedoc to Lodi, exceptional bottles are coming from every corner of the world at prices that make exploring new regions feel almost consequence-free.

Emerging and overlooked regions often have lower land costs, less market awareness and, as a result, some of the best quality-to-price ratios in the game. That’s why I don’t think of this list simply as an entry point. It’s a guide to finding your next favorite wine region before everyone else does.

Maybe that’s Oregon’s Umpqua Valley, Chile’s Leyda Valley, or New York’s Seneca Lake. This list is full of diamonds waiting to be discovered. Wine is, after all, the ultimate hobby for anyone who loves finding the indie brand nobody else has heard of. These bottles are the deep cuts, and you can explore them for $20 or less.

That’s what makes this particular list so exciting every year. Wine Enthusiast’s Tasting Panel tastes across every wine region under the sun in a way no other publication does. That breadth allows us to find not only the great bottles everyone already knows, but also the far-flung wines most people haven’t encountered yet.

So dive in before they proverbially “sell out.” Try a 92-point Beaujolais-Villages for $18, or a dry amber wine from Romania. Find the next bottle you won’t stop telling your friends about. And when everyone else finally catches on, we’ll back you up when you say you liked it before it was cool.
